chapters.title: Advertisement.
paragraphs: This short treatise comes from a far larger work that I once began without properly judging whether my abilities were equal to it. I abandoned that project long ago. I have thought it appropriate to publish only this extract, as the part of the whole that seemed least open to objection.

chapters.title: Book I. Introduction.
paragraphs: In this treatise I intend to examine whether the nature of society allows government to operate by any settled and fair principles, taking human beings as they actually are and laws as they could be framed. Throughout the inquiry I shall try to keep natural right together with the public interest, so that what is just and what is useful never become separate concerns.

Having stated my aim, I shall begin without a speech about the subject's importance. Someone might ask what business I have writing about politics: am I a prince, or do I make laws? I hold neither position; that is precisely why I am writing. Were I a ruler or lawgiver, explaining what ought to happen would be a waste of my hours. I would put the necessary measures into effect myself, or else keep silent.

I was born a citizen in a free state and a participant in its supreme authority. However little my individual vote may affect public business, my entitlement to cast it is enough to make studying that business my duty. And I count myself fortunate that, as I examine the different kinds of government, each day supplies fresh grounds for admiring the government of my own country!
Geneva.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. I. The subject of the first book.
paragraphs: A human being enters life with freedom, yet subjection is found everywhere. A man may even imagine that he rules and owns other people when his own loss of liberty is only more conspicuous than theirs. How has this transformation come about? Can anything give it a legitimate basis? I cannot settle the first of these questions, but I believe I can answer the second.

If I considered nothing beyond power's existence and its effects, I would say this: while a people is forced into obedience, obeying is sensible; once resistance becomes possible, throwing off the restraint is better still. When they reclaim their freedom on the very ground on which it was taken away, either they are entitled to reclaim it, or those who took it never had an entitlement to do so. Yet society's very nature establishes an inviolable right on which every other right rests. Human beings do not receive it directly from nature, however: it rests on an agreement between them. Our inquiry must therefore turn to the kind of agreement this could have been. Before arguing that question, though, I need to establish the claims I have already put forward.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. II. On the primitive state of society.
paragraphs: The family is the oldest human association, and the sole association that arises from nature. Even within it, however, children remain bound to their father only for as long as his help is necessary to them. Once that need ends, the natural bond dissolves of itself. The children are released from their duty to obey him, just as he is released from his duty to care for them; each becomes independent of the other. They can certainly go on living together afterwards, but then their connection rests on choice rather than nature. Even the continuing union of a family therefore depends upon an agreement freely made by its members.

The freedom shared by all human beings necessarily follows from what we are. Self-preservation is the first law of our nature, and our foremost concerns consequently relate to ourselves. As soon as a person is old enough to exercise judgment, he alone is qualified to decide how his own preservation should be secured. He therefore becomes his own master.

We can thus find the earliest pattern of political association in the family. The father corresponds to its ruler, and his children to the people. All are born equally free, so any surrender of their freedom can be justified only by their shared interest. The difference between a family and a state amounts to this: a father's natural affection for his children rewards him for the care he gives them, whereas a ruler takes pleasure in exercising command. That pleasure replaces an affection for the people that the ruler does not possess.

Grotius disputes the view that governing power exists entirely for the advantage of the governed; he points to slavery as his example. Indeed, his usual procedure is to take what happens in practice as the foundation for what is right. A different method might have proved more convincing, though it could hardly have served tyrannical government better.

"Scholarly inquiries into natural and international law often amount merely to chronicles of longstanding abuses. To become excessively attached to studying them is therefore a ridiculous delusion." Manuscript Treatise on the Interests of France, by the Marquis d' A. That observation describes Grotius's case exactly.

On Grotius's account, then, it remains uncertain whether nearly all humanity belongs to roughly a hundred people, or whether that handful belongs to humanity as a whole. Throughout his work he seems inclined to the first position. Hobbes takes the same view. They accordingly divide our species into groups resembling cattle herds, with a keeper assigned to each. The keeper shields his herd from outsiders only so that he can claim it as his own possession.

A shepherd belongs to a higher order of being than the animals he tends. On the same reasoning, those who keep human herds—their rulers—must belong to a higher order than the people under their charge. According to Philo, this was Emperor Caligula's argument. His conclusion followed logically enough from the comparison: either rulers were divine beings, or the people they ruled were merely animals.

Caligula's reasoning closely resembles the arguments put forward by Hobbes and Grotius. Aristotle had already maintained, before either of those writers, that human beings were unequal by nature: some came into life destined for enslavement, while others were destined to exercise mastery.

Aristotle correctly described what existed, but treated its result as its cause. A man who enters life in enslavement is certainly born into a slave's condition. People living under it even cease to want freedom; they choose submission, just as Ulysses' companions chose their animal condition. If there are people who seem naturally enslaved, then, that is because they were first enslaved against nature. Force created the earliest slaves, and cowardice has kept slavery in existence.
Consult Plutarch's short treatise concerning the reasoning powers of animals.

I have left King Adam and Emperor Noah out of my discussion. Noah fathered three monarchs who divided the earth between them, like Saturn's children, with whom some have identified them. I hope I deserve a little credit for my restraint here. After all, I descend directly from one of those princes, probably through the family's eldest line. Who can tell whether a properly traced genealogy might establish me as the rightful successor to a monarchy embracing the whole world? However that may be, no one can dispute Adam's claim to rule the earth while he alone inhabited it: his claim was as sound as Robinson Crusoe's claim to his island in the equivalent circumstances. Their governments also enjoyed a considerable advantage. Each monarch could occupy his throne securely, with no danger of warfare, plots against him, or revolt.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. III. On the right of the Strongest.
paragraphs: Even the strongest cannot keep his mastery for ever through strength alone. He must turn his power into an entitlement to command, and turn submission into an obligation. From this comes the supposed right attached to superior strength: apparently a phrase used in mockery, yet in practice treated as an established principle. Will anyone ever give it its proper meaning? At its simplest, force is physical power, and I cannot see how its effects produce any moral claim. Giving way to greater force is something necessity imposes, rather than a voluntary act; at most it is a sensible precaution. How, then, can we describe it as a duty?

Still, let us briefly assume this alleged right exists, and see what insoluble absurdities follow. If possession of power establishes a right, any change in the cause changes the result. Each new power that exceeds the previous one inherits its supposed entitlement. People can therefore legitimately refuse obedience as soon as they can escape punishment for doing so. Since the right invariably belongs to the stronger party, their only task is to obtain the greater strength. But what sort of right disappears the moment its holder cannot enforce it? When obedience is secured solely through compulsion, declaring it a duty serves no purpose: when the compulsion ends, so does the obligation. In this argument, therefore, adding the word right to the word force contributes nothing. Right becomes a term with no meaning of its own.

We are told to obey the powers above us. If this instruction means submitting to greater force, it offers sound but unnecessary advice; I guarantee that such a rule will never be broken. I acknowledge that every power comes from God. Every bodily illness comes from that source too; does that forbid us to summon a doctor? Suppose a robber halts me on the road. Force obliges me to hand him my purse, but does conscience oblige me as well, even if I could keep it hidden from him? Hardly anyone would claim that. Yet the pistol pressed against my chest certainly represents a force greater than my own.

We must therefore reach this conclusion: power by itself establishes no entitlement, and our obligation to obey extends only to legitimate authority. Once again, the argument brings us back to the question with which I began.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. IV. On slavery.
paragraphs: Nobody possesses authority over other human beings by nature, and sheer power creates no entitlement to rule. Agreement between people must therefore provide the foundation for every legitimate exercise of authority.

Grotius asks: if one person can give up his freedom and place himself in slavery to a master, why should a people not collectively surrender theirs to a king? Several words in this proposition are ambiguous and need explaining, but I shall concentrate on alienation, or giving something up. What we alienate is transferred either as a gift or through a sale. A man who becomes another man's slave does not make a gift of himself: he sells himself, at least in exchange for his keep. But what would induce an entire people to sell themselves? A king does not provide his subjects with their livelihood; they provide his. And, as our friend Rabelais observes, a king needs a good deal to live on. Are subjects supposed to surrender their freedom on the understanding that whoever receives it may take their property too? I truly cannot see what would remain to them after that.

One may reply that a monarch preserves peace among his subjects. Granted; but what do they gain if his ambitious wars, his limitless greed, or his ministers' oppression destroy more than internal conflicts would? What have they gained if that very peace helps make them miserable? A prisoner may find his dungeon perfectly peaceful, but is that enough to make him satisfied with living there? The Greeks imprisoned in the Cyclops' cave were left undisturbed while each awaited his turn to be eaten.

The claim that a person can give himself away is both meaningless and absurd. Such a transaction would necessarily lack legal force and validity, if only because it would show that the person making it had lost his reason. To make the same claim about a people is therefore to imagine an entire nation losing its senses at once. Even if that happened, madness could establish no right.

Even supposing a man could give himself away, he could not dispose of his children on the same terms. As human beings they enter life free; that freedom belongs to them, and only they can decide what to do with it. Until they can exercise their own judgment, a father may indeed agree on arrangements for their preservation, acting in their name and for their security. But he cannot surrender them unconditionally and beyond recall. Such a gift would contradict nature's intention and overstep paternal authority. For arbitrary government to become legitimate, each succeeding generation would therefore have to remain free to accept or refuse its authority. Under that condition, however, it would cease to be arbitrary government.

Giving up the liberty we possess by nature means giving up our very existence as human beings: we abandon humanity's obligations along with its entitlements. What compensation could possibly repay someone who surrendered everything he had? Such a surrender contradicts our nature, since removing freedom from the will removes the moral character of our actions. An agreement granting unrestricted authority to one party and requiring unquestioning obedience from the other is therefore self-defeating and contradictory. How could we owe any reciprocal duty to someone from whom we were entitled to demand everything? Since nothing on his side could balance that claim, does this not necessarily make the agreement invalid? What could my slave claim from me when I owned both him and everything he possessed? Anything he claimed would already belong to me. The suggestion that he could assert such a claim against me is absurd.

Grotius, along with other authors, finds another origin for this alleged entitlement in success on the battlefield. Their reasoning is that the victor may execute the defeated man, who may in turn legitimately buy survival by giving up freedom. They regard this bargain as particularly justifiable because each side gains something from it.

Yet the alleged entitlement of a conqueror to dispose of defeated people's lives certainly does not follow naturally from warfare in any form. One reason alone makes that clear. While human beings lived in their original independence, their relations with each other lacked the permanence needed to establish either peace or war as a condition. People consequently cannot be enemies by nature. War originates in relations concerning things, rather than relations between persons. Because its basis is property rather than personal relations, war cannot exist between one man and another, either in natural life, where settled property does not exist, or in civil society, where laws secure everything.

Individual quarrels, clashes and duels do not establish a condition of war of this kind. As for the private combats permitted under the institutions of Lewis XI, King of France, these were simply abuses belonging to feudal government. That system was thoroughly absurd, conflicting as much with sound policy as with the principles of natural justice.

War therefore concerns states in their relations with other states. Individuals become enemies only incidentally, in their capacity as soldiers. Neither their humanity nor even their citizenship makes them enemies; their role is that of defenders of their community, rather than simply its members. A state's enemy, in other words, can only be another state, not individual men. Things that differ in their essential nature cannot stand in a common relationship of this kind.

The principle agrees, indeed, with accepted rules throughout history and with the unvarying conduct of every civilized nation. Announcements that war has begun are intended chiefly for subjects' information, rather than for the information of their sovereigns.

An outsider may be a ruler, an ordinary person or a whole nation: if he plunders a subject, kills him or makes him a prisoner without announcing war upon his prince, his conduct is robbery rather than enemy action. Even when hostilities are underway, a prince acting justly may take the public possessions of the hostile country but will leave private people and their belongings secure. He thereby acknowledges the entitlements that support his own position. Warfare seeks the destruction of a hostile state. It permits the killing of that state's armed defenders; once those defenders give up their weapons, however, they no longer act as enemies or agents of hostility. Their status is simply that of human beings, and murdering them has no justification whatsoever. Indeed, destroying a state can sometimes be achieved without killing even a single person belonging to it. No wartime privilege can extend beyond what accomplishing war's purpose requires. Admittedly, Grotius does not supply these principles, nor do citations from poets establish their authority. They are conclusions reason draws from the matter's own nature.

The supposed entitlement arising from conquest has no basis except force—the rule that assigns everything to superior strength. But if victory in war gives no permission to slaughter the defeated, this nonexistent permission cannot establish a right to enslave them. If killing an enemy is permissible only when force cannot reduce him to slavery, permission to enslave him can never be based on permission to kill him. It is consequently an unjust bargain to charge him his freedom for a life we have no right to take. To ground a power of life and death in a right to enslave, and then ground the right to enslave in that power of life and death, plainly traps us in circular reasoning.

Suppose, nonetheless, that this appalling entitlement to wholesale slaughter did exist. I still maintain that a person enslaved through defeat in war, or a conquered nation reduced to slavery, owes the master nothing except obedience while he can enforce it. By accepting something in exchange for their lives, the victor does them no kindness. Instead of destroying them by useless killing, he merely adopts another form of destruction that benefits him. He therefore acquires no additional authority over them; the condition of war continues exactly as before. Their relationship is its evident consequence, and his exercise of wartime rights shows that no peace treaty has replaced it. Someone may insist that they have reached an agreement. Very well: that agreement amounts to a truce. Far from terminating the war between them, it necessarily assumes that the war continues.

However we approach the question, then, the supposed entitlement to enslave people has no validity: it is not merely unjust but absurd and meaningless. Slavery and justice contradict one another; either excludes the other. The following offer would accordingly be equally ridiculous whether addressed by one private person to another or by an individual to an entire people: I propose an agreement whose costs fall entirely on you and whose benefits are entirely mine. I shall keep it for as long as it suits me, and you must keep it for as long as I choose.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. V. On the necessity of recurring always to the primitive convention.
paragraphs: Even if I conceded everything I have so far refuted, the defender of despotism would gain little. Bringing a multitude into subjection remains very different from governing an associated people. Suppose any number of individuals, taken separately and one after another, fall under one man's control. We have only slaves and their master, not a people with its leader. Call them an accumulation if you like; they still do not form an association. Neither a commonwealth nor a political body exists among them. Even if the master acquired half the globe, he would remain a private person. His interest, distinct and separate from theirs, would remain purely private too. At his death, moreover, the empire he controlled would dissolve, leaving its parts wholly disconnected, as an oak becomes a pile of ashes when fire consumes it.

Grotius says that a people can voluntarily give themselves to a king. His own statement therefore implies that they already constitute a people before surrendering to royal authority. Even this supposed gift is a social act: it assumes that they have publicly considered the question. Before examining the act through which a people choose their king, we should consequently investigate the act through which they became a people at all. This earlier act necessarily precedes the other, and supplies society's true foundation.

Without an agreement made beforehand, why should the smaller group be bound to accept what the larger group chooses—except, of course, where everybody has voted alike? Imagine a hundred people who want a master and ten who do not. What entitles the hundred to decide for those ten? Majority voting itself rests on an agreed arrangement. It therefore assumes that the participants have, on at least one occasion, all been of one mind.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VI. On the social pact or covenant.
paragraphs: Imagine that humanity has reached a point where the obstacles to surviving in natural independence exceed what individuals can overcome through their own efforts. At that critical moment the original condition of human life could no longer continue. Unless human beings changed how they lived, their species would have perished.

Human beings cannot bring new powers into existence; they can only combine and direct powers that already exist. Their sole means of survival is therefore to unite, gathering sufficient force to overcome the obstacles threatening their security, and setting it in motion through an initiating power that can make its parts act together.

This combined power requires many separate forces to cooperate. Yet each person's strength and freedom are his main means of preserving himself. How can he commit them to the common interest without damaging his own interests and neglecting what he owes himself? Applied to our present inquiry, this difficulty becomes the problem stated immediately below.

"We must discover a way of associating in which the community's combined strength safeguards each individual's person and possessions, while every participant, though joining with everyone else, continues to obey himself alone and retains the full freedom he had previously." This is the central problem answered by the social compact.

The nature of the agreement fixes its terms so precisely that the smallest limitation or alteration deprives them of validity and effect. Although they may never have been formally announced, they remain the same everywhere, universally accepted and acknowledged without being spoken. If the social pact is broken, however, individuals regain their natural freedom and recover their original rights. They lose the freedom established by agreement, for whose sake they had surrendered those earlier rights.

Properly understood, all these terms amount to a single requirement: every person hands himself over, together with all his entitlements and privileges, to the entire community. To begin with, because everyone makes a complete surrender without holding anything back, everyone occupies the same position. No individual therefore has an interest in making their shared relationship oppressive to anyone else.

A further consequence of withholding nothing is that the resulting union achieves the greatest possible completeness. An individual participant retains no separate claim to recover. Suppose instead that particular privileges were reserved to each: no shared arbiter would then exist to settle his differences with the public. Someone entitled to decide certain cases for himself would eventually demand the same entitlement in every case. The condition of natural independence would thus continue, and their association could only end in oppression or in having no effect.

Finally, whoever gives himself to the whole does not give himself to any particular person. He obtains over every other member exactly the entitlement he grants them over himself. He consequently receives an equivalent for what he contributes, together with greater power to safeguard what he keeps.

Remove everything inessential from the social compact, and its terms become these: "Together and individually, we who make this agreement place ourselves and our capacities under the supreme guidance of the will we share as a whole. Acting collectively, we accept every member as an inseparable part of that whole."

This agreement transforms the separate people making it into a single collective moral body. It has a member for every vote in the assembly, and the agreement gives it both its unity and its existence. The public person created by everyone's union was formerly called a CITY; today it is called a republic or a body politic. Its members call it the state when it is passive and the sovereign when it acts. Compared with other bodies of the same kind, it is simply a power. As for the participants, taken together they are the people. Individually they are citizens in their capacity as sharers in sovereign authority, and subjects in their capacity as people governed by the state's laws. These terms are frequently muddled and substituted for one another. What matters, however, is being able to distinguish them when precise usage is required.

Modern usage has almost entirely distorted this word's true sense. Most people confuse a town with a city and a householder with a citizen. They fail to understand that houses can make a town, whereas only citizens can constitute a city. This very confusion once cost the Carthaginians dearly. I cannot recall ever finding the title Cives applied to a prince's subjects in anything I have read—not to the Macedonians in antiquity, nor to the English today, although they come nearer to freedom than any other nation. Only the French regularly call themselves citizens, because they lack a clear understanding of the word, as their dictionaries show. If they understood it, claiming the title would indeed constitute high treason. For them it expresses a virtue more than a privilege. Thus Bodin made a miserable blunder when, discussing Geneva's citizens and inhabitants, he confused the two. Mr. d'Alembert has avoided that error in the Encyclopoedia. He correctly distinguishes the four classes found in our city—or five, if we include mere foreigners—only two of which make up the republic. I know of no other French author who has grasped what citizen means.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VII. Of the sovereign.
paragraphs: The stated formula shows that association commits private persons and the public to obligations towards one another. Each participant enters an agreement with himself, if I may put it that way, and becomes bound in two capacities. His share in sovereign authority binds him towards particular individuals; his membership of the state binds him towards its sovereign. Here, however, we cannot apply the civil-law maxim releasing people from obligations they undertake to themselves. Promising something to oneself personally is very different from promising it to a collective whole in which one has a share.

A further point follows. A public decision binds the subject in relation to the sovereign because each person has entered the agreement in two capacities. For the opposite reason it does not bind the supreme authority in relation to itself. Consequently, the nature of the political body is incompatible with that authority imposing upon itself a law it cannot alter or break. The sovereign stands in just one relation here, occupying the position of an individual who makes an agreement with himself. No fundamental law therefore does, or can, bind an entire people in this way; even the social compact is no exception. This does not mean, however, that the body cannot make commitments to others on matters consistent with that compact. In dealings with anything outside itself, it acts as a single, individual person.

Yet the body politic, or sovereign, owes its very existence to this inviolable agreement. It cannot lawfully make any commitment, even to another body of the same kind, that conflicts with the original act's terms—for example, giving away part of itself or surrendering wholly to a foreign sovereign. Breaking the act that constitutes its existence would destroy that existence, and nothing can emerge from nothing.

Once numerous individuals unite in this way, an attack on any member necessarily attacks the entire body; still more plainly, an attack on the body injures its members. Both obligation and self-interest therefore require the two parties to support one another. The same people, acting in these two capacities, ought to seek all the advantages their double relationship can provide.

The sovereign consists solely of the individuals who make up the state, so it cannot have an interest opposed to theirs. The supreme authority consequently needs to provide its subjects with no guarantee: the body cannot harm all the members of which it consists. Later we shall see that it can no more tend towards harming any individual member. Its very existence thus necessarily makes the sovereign what it ought to be.

The subjects' relationship to the sovereign is different. Despite their common interest, the sovereign has no assurance that they will honour their commitments unless some means can be found to secure their faithfulness to them.

Consider someone in his private human capacity: he may want something quite unlike, or directly contrary to, what he wills collectively as a citizen. Personal advantage can pull him in precisely the reverse direction from society's welfare. He sees his separate existence as real and naturally independent, and may therefore regard his contribution to the common undertaking as an optional donation. To him, the harm others suffer if he withholds it may seem smaller than the burden he would bear by providing it. Moreover, since the state's moral personality is not an actual human being, he may dismiss it as something imaginary. He would then want to claim every benefit of being a citizen while evading the obligations that belong to being a subject. As this injustice develops, it necessarily brings the political body to ruin.

For the social compact to have substance, it therefore silently contains one commitment that alone makes the others enforceable: anyone who refuses to follow the general will can be required to do so by the community's combined force. In effect, this means that compulsion may secure his freedom. By attaching each citizen to the state, this condition protects him from dependence on any private person. The entire construction and operation of the political system rests on it. It alone makes the obligations of social life fair and just; without it, those obligations would be senseless, oppressive and open to the most monstrous abuses.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VIII. Of civil society in general.
paragraphs: Passing from natural independence into organized society profoundly changes a human being. Justice replaces instinct as the rule of conduct, and actions acquire a moral character they previously lacked. When the call of duty takes the place of bodily impulses and the rule of appetite, someone who formerly considered only his own gratification discovers that he must act on other principles. He must consult reason before following his passions. Joining society certainly deprives him of many advantages belonging to natural life. But the advantages he receives in exchange are immense: his faculties find employment and develop, his ideas widen, his feelings become nobler, and his whole spirit rises to a higher level. Unless abuses within this new condition drag him below his former one, he ought continually to bless the fortunate moment that rescued him from it. That moment transformed him from an unthinking, ignorant animal into a being capable of intelligence and wisdom.

We can set out the losses and gains by placing them side by side. In making the social compact, a person relinquishes his natural freedom: an unrestricted claim to whatever he wants and can obtain. In exchange he receives civil freedom and exclusive ownership of all the things currently in his possession. To understand this exchange correctly, however, we must distinguish two kinds of liberty. Natural liberty ends only at the limits of what an individual is capable of doing; civil liberty is bounded by the community's general will. We must likewise distinguish possession, maintained simply by force or following from first occupation, from property, which rests solely upon an established title.

We may add another gain from living in society: moral freedom, which alone gives a person true command of himself. To follow appetite and nothing else is a form of enslavement; freedom consists in obeying laws we lay down for ourselves. But I have already gone further into this subject than I should. The philosophical meaning of Liberty lies outside the question being considered here.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. IX. Of real demesnes.
paragraphs: On joining the community, each member commits himself to the public as he then stands, with all his powers and capacities, including the possessions that form part of those capacities. This does not mean that transferring possession changes its nature, turning it into genuine property in the sovereign's hands. Rather, because the community's strength is incomparably greater than an individual's, public possession is in practice more secure and harder to reverse, without becoming more legitimate—at least in relation to foreigners. In relation to its own members, every state controls their possessions by virtue of the social compact, which provides the foundation for all other rights within it. In relation to other powers or states, however, its claim rests only on first occupation, a claim it receives from the individuals concerned.

A claim based on occupying something first has more substance than one based on superior force, but becomes a just entitlement only after property has been established. Nature gives every person a claim to whatever he needs to live. Yet the definite act that makes him the owner of a particular holding excludes him from ownership of other holdings. Once his share has been allotted, he should restrict himself to it, and can no longer claim common possession of everything. This explains why first occupation, which counts for little in natural life, commands such respect in society. In considering the claim, our attention is directed chiefly towards what belongs to someone else, rather than simply towards what is not ours.

In general, a claim based on first occupation requires the following conditions. First, the land in question must not already be occupied by anybody else. Second, the area occupied must be no larger than the occupants need to support themselves. Third, taking possession must involve actual cultivation, rather than an empty ceremony. Where legal titles are lacking, cultivation is the only indication of property deserving recognition.

Allowing the first occupant as much land as he can cultivate and needs for his support takes the claim as far as reason permits. Otherwise, we cannot tell where to set its limits. Does merely stepping onto an uninhabited territory immediately entitle someone to exclude everyone else? If he can once drive others away by force, does that deprive them for ever of permission to return? How could an individual, or even an entire people, seize an enormous territory and bar the rest of humanity without committing an unlawful usurpation? They would thereby deny others a home and the means of living that nature has provided for everyone in common. When Nunez Balbao stood beside the sea and claimed the Pacific Ocean and all South-America for the crown of Castile, was that ceremony enough to dispossess all the inhabitants of that vast country and exclude every other sovereign anywhere in the world? If so, these pointless ceremonies could have been repeated to a ridiculous extent. His Catholic Majesty need only have claimed the entire world while sitting in his private room, then subtracted from his empire whatever other princes already possessed.

It is easy to understand how neighbouring individual estates, joined together, become public territory. Sovereign authority extends from the subjects to their holdings and thus acquires a claim over both people and land. This places possessors in the greatest dependence, making even their own resources a guarantee of their loyalty. Ancient rulers seem not to have appreciated this advantage fully. Calling themselves kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians, they apparently regarded themselves as leaders of people rather than masters of a country. Modern princes show greater cunning in calling themselves kings of England, France, Spain, and so forth. By claiming the territory itself, they make sure of its inhabitants.

This surrender has a remarkable feature. By accepting individuals' possessions, the community does not strip them of those possessions. On the contrary, it strengthens their hold, turning usurpation into a genuine entitlement and simple possession into actual property. The possessors are also regarded as custodians of the public wealth. Every member of the state respects their rights, and its entire force defends those rights against foreign powers. Through a surrender beneficial to the public and still more beneficial to themselves, they thus acquire, so to speak, everything they surrendered. The paradox is readily explained by distinguishing the sovereign's rights over the same property from its owner's rights, as we shall see later.

People may also come together in a society before owning anything. After acquiring a territory sufficient to provide for all of their members, they may hold it jointly or divide it into shares, whether equal or unequal, as the sovereign decides. However the acquisition occurs, each person's entitlement to his particular estate must always remain subordinate to the community's entitlement over everyone's possessions. Without that subordination, the social bond would impose no binding obligation, and the exercise of supreme authority would have no effective force.

I shall close this book with an observation that should underpin the entire social system. Far from abolishing human beings' natural equality, the founding compact establishes moral and legal equality to compensate for their natural and physical differences. People may possess unequal bodily strength and unequal intellectual abilities, yet agreement and right make them equals within the association.

Under some governments this equality is only a deceptive appearance, serving to keep poor people miserable and to favour oppression by the rich. Laws in fact always benefit those with wealth and injure those who have nothing. Society therefore benefits humanity generally only when everyone owns something and no individual among them possesses an excessively large share.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. I. That the sovereignty is unalienable.
paragraphs: The first and most important conclusion from the principles established so far is this: only the general will can guide the state's forces towards the purpose for which it was founded, namely the common good. Conflicting private interests may have made society necessary, but agreement between those interests must have made society possible. Its bonds must have arisen from something those different interests shared; without any point at which they could be reconciled, no society could have existed. Those shared points alone, therefore, should provide the basis on which society is governed.

Sovereignty, I maintain, consists only in exercising the general will and therefore cannot be handed over. The sovereign is a collective being, which can speak for itself alone: a people can transfer or delegate its power, but cannot transfer its will.

An individual's wishes might conceivably coincide with the general will on a particular issue. Such agreement cannot, however, be permanent or assured: private wishes always tend to favour particular people or things, whereas the general will tends towards complete equality. Even supposing the agreement could persist indefinitely, guaranteeing it would be still more impossible. Chance, rather than deliberate arrangement, would account for it. A sovereign may say: at this moment I will what that individual wills, or at least what he claims to will. It cannot say in advance: I consent to whatever that individual will want tomorrow, regardless of what he might then decide. For the will to impose such a restraint upon its future is absurd, and it cannot consent to anything opposed to the interest of the being whose will it is. A people that merely pledged obedience would therefore cease, through that very act, to exist as a people. Once a master appears, sovereign authority disappears, because the political body itself has been destroyed.

This does not mean that a chief's commands cannot be treated as expressions of the general will where the sovereign leaves them unopposed despite remaining free to contradict them. In those circumstances, the people's universal silence can be taken as consent. I shall explain this point further towards the end.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. II. That the sovereignty is indivisible.
paragraphs: What makes sovereignty impossible to transfer also makes it impossible to divide. Either a will is general or it is not: it belongs to the people collectively or merely to a section of them. In the former case, its declaration exercises sovereign authority and establishes a law. In the latter, it expresses a particular will, or an act of administration, and amounts at most to a decree.
Generality does not always require unanimous agreement. It does require that every person be allowed to cast a vote: excluding anyone by formal rule damages the will's general character.

Unable to divide sovereignty at the level of its basic principles, our political writers divide it according to the matters it deals with. They distinguish will from power, legislation from execution, the powers of taxation from those of administering justice or conducting war, and domestic business from foreign affairs. Sometimes they jumble these together; sometimes they treat each as separate. Their sovereign becomes a fantastical composite, like a man put together from several bodies, one consisting entirely of eyes, another entirely of arms, a third entirely of feet. Japanese conjurers, we are told, cut up a child before their audience and toss the severed limbs into the air, one after another. The pieces reunite and the child comes down alive and unharmed. Our modern political writers perform much the same feat. Having skilfully dismembered the political body, they bring its pieces together again by magic and announce that it is just what it was before.

Their mistake comes from failing to define sovereign authority precisely. They confuse consequences flowing from that authority with essential parts of the authority itself. Declaring war and making peace, for example, are commonly classed as acts of sovereignty, but neither is one. Neither makes a law: each applies a law. Each is a particular act deciding only what the law means in the case concerned. This will become clearer once we have settled exactly what we mean by the word law.

Examining their other divisions in the same way reveals the same mistake whenever sovereignty appears to be divided. The powers supposedly forming its separate parts are all subordinate to it. They presuppose an earlier decision by a higher will, whose determination those powers serve merely to carry out.

It is impossible to measure how much confusion this imprecision has introduced into writers' arguments about political law when they assess kings' and peoples' respective rights according to their chosen principles. Consider chapters three and four in the first book of Grotius. There the reader can see the learned author and his translator, Barbeyrac, becoming lost in their own deceptive arguments. They fear saying either too much or too little for their purposes, or setting against one another the interests they are trying to reconcile. Displeased with his countrymen, living as a refugee in France, and wishing to please Lewis XIII, to whom he dedicated the book, Grotius used every device and effort to deprive peoples of privileges and confer prerogatives upon kings. Barbeyrac pursued a similar aim when he dedicated his translation to England's George I. Unfortunately for him, James II's expulsion—which he describes as an abdication—required great caution and repeated evasions if William III was not to emerge as a usurper. Sound principles would have removed all these difficulties and allowed both writers to reason consistently. But then, in sober earnest, they would merely have told the truth and sought the people's favour. Truth-telling does not make fortunes; the populace appoints no ambassadors and has no offices or pensions to distribute.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. III. Whether the general Will can be in the wrong.
paragraphs: The argument so far shows that the general will is invariably right and directed towards public welfare. That does not mean the people's deliberations will invariably be equally sound. We always want what benefits us, but do not always recognize where that benefit lies. A people taken as a whole cannot become corrupt, although it can often be mistaken. Only in that situation does it appear to pursue what harms it.

What every member wills, added together, often differs considerably from what the whole body wills generally. The general will looks solely to shared interests; the other total reflects individuals' private interests and simply adds their separate wishes together. Remove from that total the opposed wishes that cancel one another, however, and the differences left over, taken together, form the general will.

The Marquis d'A. remarks that different interests proceed from different principles: two separate interests may join forces because both oppose a third. He might equally have remarked that everyone's interests join forces by opposing each person's individual interest. If interests neither differed nor clashed, the common interest would face no obstacle and would scarcely be perceptible as such. Affairs would run smoothly by themselves, and the management of civil society would no longer be an art.

Imagine citizens who understand the question being considered and reach their judgments independently, without consulting one another. The many small differences between their views would invariably yield the general will, making their deliberation sound. Once conspiracies develop, however, and sectional organizations are established at the expense of society as a whole, each organization's wishes count as general for the people within it but as particular when considered in relation to the state. We could then say that there are no longer individual voices corresponding to individual people: only the organizations have voices. Differences become fewer, and the outcome less general. Suppose, moreover, that one organization becomes powerful enough to sway every other one. Instead of numerous minor differences being added together, a single great difference determines the result. Under those circumstances, there can no longer be a general will.

For each resolution to express the general will, then, the state must contain no such sectional associations, and every citizen must judge independently. This was the lofty principle instituted by the great Lycurgus. If smaller associations are nevertheless bound to exist, the sensible precaution is to make them numerous and prevent inequalities between them, as Solon, Numa and Servius did. Only these beneficial precautions can ensure that the general will is properly informed and that the people do not misunderstand where their true interest lies.

Machiavel says: It is true that some divisions damage republics while others help them. Those accompanied by factions and partisan followers do damage; those maintained without factions or partisan followers help. Since a republic's founder cannot ensure that no hostilities arise within it, he must at least ensure that factions do not arise. History of Florence, book vii.
